sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Pittsburgh
sections.html:
Pittsburgh owners deal with three taxing bodies: the city, the school district and Allegheny County. The city's Real Estate Division bills and collects the city tax, while the county sets the assessed value that every rate is applied to. The tax applies to all owners of real estate within the city and school district, and it is the millage rate multiplied by the assessed value.

The Real Estate Division sits at 414 Grant Street and answers at 412-255-2525. Chapter 263 of the Pittsburgh Code covers the tax. Bills usually go out in the middle of January, with installment bills mailed in April and July.

The county's role is separate. The Allegheny County Office of Property Assessments decides what your house is worth for tax purposes, and the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review hears disputes. If your bill looks wrong, work out whether the problem is the value (a county matter) or the payment record (a city matter) before you call anyone.

The year's bill can be paid in one amount or in three installments, and the dates repeat every year.

  • February 10: last day to take the 2 percent discount, on either the full annual amount or the first installment
  • February 27: first installment due, or the annual amount at its gross figure
  • April 30: second installment due
  • July 31: third installment due

The first installment is where people get caught. A payment that misses the end of February, or falls short of the whole first installment, makes the entire year's tax due, with interest running from March 1. An online payment portal run by Magic Collection Solutions is linked from the city's tax page.

A taxpayer who misses the discount can ask for an extension using the discount extension form on the city's Real Estate Forms page.

Three rates stack on a Pittsburgh bill. For 2026 they are 6.43 mills for the county, 9.67 for the city and 10.457 for the school district, a combined 26.557 mills. In 2025 the city rate was 8.06 and the county rate was 6.43, and in 2024 the county rate was 4.73. The taxable residential median value is $68,600.

A buyer will estimate the bill from the assessment and these rates, so a seller who has the assessed value and the rates in hand can answer that question early.

Value disputes go to the Allegheny County Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review, which sits outside city government. The board now handles scheduling and hearing notices on its own.

Annual appeals are filed in a summer window. The most recent one ran from July 1 to September 1. A person who misses it may file under limited circumstances, but first has to submit a late-filed appeal form. Call the county before the next window opens.

  • Residential hearing notices are mailed at least 14 days ahead; commercial notices at least 21 days ahead.
  • The board meets every two weeks at 8:00 am in Room 328 of the County Office Building, 542 Forbes Avenue.
  • The 2027 common level ratio is 49.3 percent, and it applies to current market value in appeals heard starting September 2026.

An appeal compares the assessed value with market value after that ratio is applied. Bring recent comparable sales and any repair estimates to the hearing.

Two measures are meant to lower a city bill: the Act 50 homestead exemption of $15,000 and the Act 77 senior tax relief, a 40 percent reduction on assessment.

Eligibility rules, forms and filing dates come from the county and city offices, so ask the Real Estate Division or the Office of Property Assessments before you assume a reduction applies to your parcel.

sections.h2: Selling a Pittsburgh house with back taxes
sections.html:
Old delinquent taxes are split between two collectors. The city keeps prior-year delinquent City, Library and Parks real estate taxes and answers questions at 412-255-2525. Prior-year delinquent school taxes were turned over to Jordan Tax Service, Inc., which takes payment arrangements at 412-345-7960.

The city's delinquency list can be downloaded by anyone, but it may not show the current owner if the county has not yet reported a transfer, may not reflect assessment changes decided on appeal, and may leave out accounts under $50. A title search is the safer check, and the payoff figure should come directly from the city and the collection agency in writing.

At settlement, the agent subtracts unpaid taxes from what the seller receives and sends the money to the collectors. If the debts exceed the price, the settlement statement shows the shortfall before anyone signs.

sections.h2: What does the transfer tax cost on a Pittsburgh sale?
sections.html:
Allegheny County realty transfer tax runs from 2 to 5 percent, and Pittsburgh sits at the top of that range. For a house in the city the total is 5 percent: 1 percent to the state, 3 percent to the city and 1 percent to the Pittsburgh School District. The city applied the 5 percent rate to residential deeds recorded starting February 1, 2020.

Payment happens at recording, on its own check apart from the recording fees. Both sides are liable under state rules, and certain transfers, such as inheritances, are exempt. The sale contract decides who actually pays.

Pittsburgh covers about 55 square miles in the center of Allegheny County, with steep slopes and floodplains along the Allegheny, Monongahela and Ohio rivers. Slope and flood exposure differ a great deal from one neighborhood to the next, which can affect price and insurance. The mid 2025 population is 307,632. Owners occupy 47.7 percent of occupied homes, so renters make up the majority of households. An owned home typically carries a $205,800 value, and median household income is $65,742.

A short list covers most of what a Pittsburgh seller needs.

  1. Gather the latest city and school bills and note whether you paid by installment or in full.
  2. Call the Real Estate Division at 412-255-2525 for a balance, and ask Jordan Tax Service, Inc. at 412-345-7960 about any prior-year school taxes.
  3. Add up the 5 percent transfer tax and decide how the contract splits it.
  4. Have a recent comparable sales list on hand in case the buyer asks why the assessment looks high or low.

A cash sale skips the listing and repair steps, but the tax payoff and transfer tax work the same way at the closing table.

faqs.q: What is the Pittsburgh discount deadline?
faqs.a: February 10. Paying the full annual tax or the first installment by that date earns a 2 percent discount. After that, the gross amount is due February 27.

faqs.q: What happens if I skip the first installment?
faqs.a: You owe the whole year at once, and interest starts March 1. The same result follows from paying less than the full first installment.

faqs.q: Where can I get answers on a Pittsburgh tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the city's Real Estate Division at 412-255-2525 or visit 414 Grant Street. Questions about the value itself belong with the Allegheny County Office of Property Assessments.

faqs.q: When can I appeal my Pittsburgh assessment?
faqs.a: Annual appeals are filed in a summer window, July 1 to September 1 in the most recent cycle. A late-filed appeal form is available under limited circumstances. Ask the county for the next window.

faqs.q: Who gets paid when a house with back taxes sells?
faqs.a: The title company pays them from the seller's proceeds. Delinquent city taxes go to the city, and prior-year school taxes go to Jordan Tax Service, Inc. Get written payoff figures first.
